rationale: A wins because it mostly keeps the story on the facts and turns missing evidence into reporting requirements instead of decorating the hole. Its strongest line, "Canva picks a fight with Adobe and Microsoft over your company's design software budget," is a real competitive angle with a beat, a peg, and proof needs. B has useful shapes, but "220 million users already inside companies" is not in the update, and that kind of confident overreach is how a founder ends up pitching fan fiction with a logo.
gaps_in_A: "Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams" compares individual monthly users to paid teams as if they are the same unit. That's a tempting chart crime, not a clean data angle.
"IT departments were blocking it for" is plausible, but not evidenced. The update says SSO and admin tools are launching; it does not say IT blocked prior adoption.

"growth funded by profit and an acquisition instead" overstates the finance story. The facts say Canva is profitable, private, valued at $26B, and acquired an AI startup; they do not explain how the expansion was funded.

"brand-safe image generation beats generic AI tools" imports a competitive and legal-risk frame the update does not prove. The set partly saves itself by asking for proof, but the headline gets ahead of the evidence.
gaps_in_B: "220 million users already inside companies" is invented. The update says Canva has 220 million monthly users, not where they work or whether they sit inside enterprise accounts.

"multi-seat contracts," "shadow IT," and "Canva is the largest consumer-originated design tool to attempt it" are unsupported. That whole PLG-to-enterprise angle may be smart, but B writes the analysis as fact.
"so the legal team can make a slide deck without asking design" creates a user, workflow, and asset type out of thin air. Good color is not a substitute for evidence.

"Enterprise contracts introduce stickier, higher-ASP revenue and reduce churn risk" is finance-speak without disclosed pricing, contract terms, churn, or customer mix. It may be true; it is not in the update.
